facts.text: Seligman earned its name in 1886 when New York banker Jesse Seligman helped finance the railroad that made the town a key stop on the Santa Fe mainline.
Before becoming Seligman, the town was called Prescott Junction because it sat where the Santa Fe mainline met the feeder line to Prescott.
The town’s historic Route 66 legacy began when trains gave way to automobiles, turning Seligman into a classic roadside stop for travelers.
The 1910 Cottage Hotel, now on the National Register of Historic Places, still stands at 1st Street and Shoney Avenue, a reminder of Seligman’s early 20th‑century boom.
At 5,240 feet above sea level, Seligman sits beside Big Chino Wash, a tributary of the Verde River that once fed the region’s early settlers.
